agree.reason: The letter is warm and well supported, so an editor who likes her would probably offer more, but a $2,500 jump over budget with an $8,000 alternative available makes a counteroffer below $11,500 more likely than full agreement.

honest.reason: It correctly drops the unsupported claim that every other publisher pays at least $12,000 and relies on the one real $12,500 data point plus the agent's range, though "full-time" and "my fees elsewhere have gone up" (based on one book) go slightly beyond the brief.

works_the_facts.reason: It states the raw facts accurately but derives nothing from them, such as the fee being flat across six books and four years, $9,000 over four months coming to about $2,250 a month, or $11,500 still being $1,000 below what she was paid elsewhere.

right_comparison.reason: It sets the flat $9,000 against the $12,500 paid elsewhere and the $11,000–$13,000 market range, but it doesn't spell out that this publisher's rate hasn't changed while the market has, and it gives no reason why her proven sales are worth more than a cheaper, untested illustrator.

qualification.reason: The document is a straightforward fee request and needs no conditional hedge.

objections.reason: The sales figures and reading-list placement answer "why pay more" only by implication, and the letter never addresses the budget ceiling or the cheaper-illustrator option by making the case that a proven seller lowers the publisher's risk.

fit.reason: It's a properly formatted email of about 200 words, well under the 250-word limit, with a clear ask and a friendly tone.
